<reason>In a high-level debate, Side A edges out the win by proving that waiting for raw-material dependence to finance its own replacement is a structural trap. While Side B made sharp microeconomic arguments regarding hard-currency constraints, high production costs, and governance failures, Side A successfully demonstrated that raw-export dependence locks infrastructure into mine-to-port enclaves while bleeding scarce foreign exchange on basic imports like refined fuel, food, and fertilizer. Furthermore, Side A exposed a core tension in Side B's case: once Side B conceded that states must tax resource rents to fund industry and bargain for local processing, Side B effectively agreed that strategic priority must shift away from raw-material dependence, leaving Side A with the cleaner case on the motion as written (despite a minor P/A reference-tag typo in Side A's closing).</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The standout exchange centered on Side B's claim [B1.3] that raw exports are needed to earn hard currency to import "fuel, medicine," and infrastructure. Side A [A2.1] brilliantly flipped this list into an indictment of the status quo—pointing out that oil-rich Nigeria and fertile African states drain foreign exchange importing refined fuel and food precisely because they prioritized raw exports over regional processing—which Side B [B2.1, B4.6] then fiercely countered by pointing to the historical failure and high costs of Nigeria's state-owned refineries.</best_rebuttal>
